arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Wilker argued the plaintiffs pled a plausible claim. He stated they alleged intentional viewpoint discrimination.
Mr. Gershengorn described the physical layout of the protest area. He noted the alley entry point on California Street.
Justice Kennedy asked if objective bases make motive irrelevant. He questioned the weight of subjective intent in such cases.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests whether officials can move protesters for safety reasons. The core issue is if subjective intent matters when objective grounds exist.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Protesters want a ruling that subjective intent matters. They seek to prove agents acted with discriminatory motives.
Agents want a ruling that objective safety justifies action. They seek dismissal of the discrimination claims.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Protesters argue agents moved them solely due to their political views. They claim this violates core First Amendment principles.
Agents argue they acted for objective safety reasons. They contend subjective motives are irrelevant if safety grounds exist.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked if objective reasons negate unconstitutional motives. He suggested the case is simple if objective grounds exist.
Justice Breyer asked if the Court should reach the intent question. He noted the distinction between ordinary police and Secret Service agents.
